advances: An integer-shape density sign at zero for a scalar law under a coefficient cap.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Let $g_k$ denote the density of $X$, equal to $x^{k-1}e^{-x}/(k-1)!$ on $x>0$ and zero on $x\le0$. It is globally Lipschitz for $k\ge2$, since it vanishes at zero and its derivative is bounded on each open half-line. The coefficient sum forces $Y>0$ almost surely. Differentiating $f(x)=\mathbb E[g_k(x+Y)]$ at zero by dominated convergence gives
$$
f'(0)=\frac{\mathbb E[e^{-Y}((k-1)Y^{k-2}-Y^{k-1})]}{(k-1)!}.
$$
This includes $k=2$, where the derivative of $g_k$ can jump at zero.

Put $\lambda_i=b_i/(1+b_i)$ and $L=\prod_i(1+b_i)^{-1}$. Tilting the joint law by $e^{-Y}/L$ replaces each nonzero exponential phase of mean $b_i$ with an independent one of mean $\lambda_i$, leaving zero phases deterministic. By the multinomial formula and the exponential moment formula, for $r\ge0$ one has $\mathbb E[e^{-Y}Y^r]=Lr!\,h_r(\lambda)$, where $h_r(\lambda)=\sum_{\sum_i n_i=r}\prod_i\lambda_i^{n_i}$ and the indices $n_i$ are nonnegative integers. A zero phase contributes only when its exponent is zero. Thus $f'(0)=L[h_{k-2}(\lambda)-h_{k-1}(\lambda)]$.

The geometric variables of means $b_i$ have sum mass function $p(r)=Lh_r(\lambda)$ because $1-\lambda_i=(1+b_i)^{-1}$. The geometric mode lemma applies at $n=k-1$, since $\mu=\sum_i b_i\ge k$ and $b_{\max}\le1$. This proves $f'(0)=p(k-2)-p(k-1)\le0$. If equality holds, the equality criterion of that lemma gives $k-1=\mu-b_{\max}$ with all positive means equal. The two coefficient bounds then force $\mu=k$ and $b_{\max}=1$, hence exactly $k$ unit phases. Conversely those phases satisfy the equality criterion.
statement: Let $k\ge2$ be an integer, let $X$ have the $\operatorname{Gamma}(k,1)$ law, and let $Y=\sum_i b_iE_i$ for finitely many unit-mean exponentials $E_i$, independent of each other and of $X$. Assume $0\le b_i\le1$ and $\sum_i b_i\ge k$. The continuous convolution density $f$ of $X-Y$ is differentiable at zero and satisfies $f'(0)\le0$. Equality holds exactly when $k$ of the $b_i$ equal one and all others equal zero.
title: Derivative at zero for a gamma law minus capped exponential phases
